frameworks.name: Three Things to Win
frameworks.definition: Success requires only three prerequisites: the courage to start (balls), the discipline to learn (brains), and the commitment to persist (heart).

frameworks.name: 20 Hour Competence Rule
frameworks.definition: Base competence in any skill (including money-making skills) requires only 20 hours of focused effort; the binding constraint is starting, not capability.

claims.text: Success requires only three prerequisites: the balls to start, the brains to learn, and the heart to never give up. Everyone already possesses all three.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Confidence is not a precondition for action; it is a retroactive result of taking action. The elimination of alternatives through commitment to continuous motion—walking the marathon even when slowed—hardens conviction over time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Repeated action generates proof of capability, which retroactively builds confidence; this compounding effect is undermined by waiting for confidence before starting.

claims.text: Most people chronically delay improvement because they assume today is not worth improving—that improvement is only justified by a special occasion. This mental model systematically pushes desired outcomes into the future indefinitely.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: The optimal time to begin working on next year's goals is now, not on January 1st. If you had a lottery ticket for the life you want, you would cash it immediately; deferring improvement is equivalent to leaving that ticket on the counter.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: When goal outcome is known and valued
claims.mechanism: Delay assumes tomorrow is guaranteed; starting now captures compound hours immediately rather than losing them to deferral.
bounded_by: Does not apply when precondition clarity is missing (you don't know if the goal is actually worth your time)

claims.text: Tomorrow is not guaranteed. This is a harsh truth that most people avoid until they are significantly older, but the sooner a person internalizes it, the sooner they stop leaving their life to chance.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Getting good at anything is not instantaneous; it takes time. However, only 20 hours of focused effort is required to achieve base competence in any skill—ads, content creation, video editing, sales. The binding constraint is not the 20 hours; it is starting the first hour.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: When focusing on base competence (not mastery)
When 20 hours of continuous, focused effort is available

numbers.axis: hours of focused practice required for base competence

anchors.region: skills baseline (ads, content, video editing, sales)

bounded_by: Does not address mastery, which requires substantially more hours
Assumes uninterrupted focus; part-time effort spreads this across calendar time

claims.text: The unknown creates anxiety because there is a nonzero possibility of negative outcomes, even when the expected value is positive. People avoid good surprises for the same reason they avoid neutral or negative ones—the common thread is the absence of control and predictability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: When outcome has not yet occurred
claims.mechanism: Uncertainty triggers threat-detection regardless of base-rate probability; humans generalize the discomfort of unknown-negative to unknown-good.

claims.text: Many people delay action because they assume negative consequences are likely even when they haven't tested. Most people could achieve next year's goals before the year ends if they began now instead of waiting.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: When goals are defined and feasible within the remaining calendar period

claims.text: The longest delay in skill acquisition is the gap between recognizing a need and starting the first hour of practice. New sales hires can be onboarded in a few days; the massive delay is psychological—people assume the unknown is bad and therefore never test it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: For trainable skills with clear instruction paths
claims.mechanism: Unknown outcome triggers assumed-negative bias, which prevents testing; once testing begins, onboarding speed reveals the psychological delay was the real bottleneck, not capability gap.

claims.text: An 85-year-old version of yourself will not remember most surprises or small setbacks from today. On a sufficiently long time horizon, almost all short-term anxiety about unknown outcomes becomes statistically irrelevant.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not apply to decisions that are truly catastrophic (health, legal, financial ruin)

examples.text: A person who wants to learn ads, content creation, video editing, or sales can achieve base competence in any of these within the calendar time between now and year-end by committing 20 hours of focused effort. The delay is not capability or complexity; it is the decision to start.

A sales hire can be onboarded from zero experience to functional productivity in a few days. The perception that onboarding takes months is driven by hidden anxiety about the unknown, not by actual training complexity.

People avoid surprise parties even when the party is designed to be good because they dislike the unknown state itself. The discomfort of uncertainty is what triggers avoidance—the valence (positive or negative) is secondary.

practices.text: Make the commitment now to never stop. Commit to continuous motion (walking the marathon) even if you must slow down or pant—the imperative is to keep moving, not to maintain initial velocity.
Vote with your action today. Make today the only day that is good because it's the only day you have control over. Do not defer improvement waiting for a special occasion or New Year's resolution.
Start your first hour in any skill immediately. Do not wait for perfect conditions, full clarity, or high confidence. The bottleneck is the decision to begin, not the capability to execute.
